channel.title: Rhinoceros — Lansing Public Records Investigations
channel.description: Public records investigations into local government, money, and power in Michigan.

item.title: What Is the Lansing Housing Commission?
item.description: The Lansing Housing Commission is the City of Lansing's public housing authority, a five-member volunteer board appointed by the Mayor under MCL 125.651. Two of the five seated commissioners hold paid positions at organizations that earn fees from LHC's development pipeline. The agency's executive director is the registered agent and organizing member of the General Partner LLCs that collect developer fees on LHC's LIHTC partnerships. The board's 2024 voting record contains one abstention out of at least fifteen substantive resolutions. Documented governance conflicts under HUD PIH Notice 2019-01 and Michigan Nonprofit Corporation Act §450.2541.

item.title: Lansing's First Flock Briefing
item.description: On April 23, 2026, Lansing Police Chief Robert Backus made the first sustained on-the-record statement about the Lansing Flock surveillance camera program in a Council-committee setting. The 32-minute discussion produced two parts of the chief's account that are inconsistent on their face and confirmed what the chief said is missing: no civilian oversight, no scheduled audit-log review, no alert when the audit log is opened, and no recorded discipline for misuse.

item.title: Lansing City Operations Committee, April 23
item.description: A 32-minute committee meeting on April 23, 2026 produced a unanimous compost proclamation, a place-on-file vote on a downtown liquor-license transfer, and the city's first sustained on-record account of the Lansing Police Department's Flock Safety camera program.

item.title: From Public Housing to Wall Street Mortgages: The Lansing Scattered-Site Sale
item.description: The Lansing Housing Commission sold 202 scattered-site public-housing homes to a Florida-linked LLC in 2023. The mortgages were assigned through Goldman Sachs Mortgage Company to a Wall Street mortgage trust. The 20-year affordability covenant runs through 2042; after that, no public-purpose constraint remains.

item.title: Lansing's Public Housing: From 833 Units to 66
item.description: How Lansing lost 92 percent of its public housing portfolio in four years, and where 202 of those homes went. Documented from HUD records, Ingham County Register of Deeds, MiCOURT, and LARA filings.

item.title: Five Patterns Inside Lansing's Housing Crisis
item.description: Five patterns repeat in Lansing's rental market: $500 fines that do not exceed monthly rent, eviction filings as a regular operating activity, mass eviction before a profitable sale, holding-company fragmentation that hides operator-scale portfolios, and code enforcement that stops at each municipal line. What the records show, what it costs renters, and the offices that can change the rules.

item.title: What the Evidence and the Record Show About Flock's Cameras
item.description: The peer-reviewed evidence for license-plate-reader networks is mixed. The 2024 to 2026 public record of Flock deployments includes wrongful detentions, officer stalking, protest and abortion-travel surveillance, and federal-agency access without local authorization. Lansing's Committee on City Operations takes up the city's Flock deployment at 4 PM today.

item.title: Who Owns and Funds the Cameras Watching Lansing
item.description: The company whose cameras operate in Lansing is a venture-capital-backed Atlanta vendor valued at $7.5 billion. The "Flock Grant system" named on the April 23 Lansing committee agenda is a grant-assistance service, not a charitable program.

item.title: Lansing's Homeowner Permit Rule for Tagged Structures
item.description: A January 9, 2026 administrative policy bars homeowners from pulling repair permits on red-tagged property until a licensed contractor completes the work removing the tag. The policy was not adopted by Council vote. A resident who had negotiated a cure path at a November hearing was denied at the permit counter.

item.title: The Shuffle Lease Does Not Oblige the City to Sell
item.description: Section (f) of the 2020 Shuffle lease says initiation is not a promise. City Attorney Greg Venker confirmed it on the record at Committee of the Whole on April 20, 2026: 'we're not bound to do this thing.' What the record supports, and what it does not.

item.title: Why Does Lansing Need Flock?
item.description: Lansing Police operate about 20 Flock Safety surveillance cameras. No public document posted by the city explains why, who authorized them, or how the program is governed. A Council committee will review it for the first time at 4 PM Thursday. Public comment is open.

item.title: Lansing City Council Meeting: April 20, 2026
item.description: A 182-day data center moratorium, introduced and referred. The Lansing Shuffle sale is headed to the August ballot on a 6-1 vote over the Park Board's no-recommend. Four liquor-store zoning ordinances passed unanimously.

item.title: Lansing's Deep Green Due Diligence Gap
item.description: Deep Green's flagship UK facility experienced three cooling failures in five months. Its only cloud customer removed the facility from public documentation. The company deleted 'heat reuse' from the facility's own webpage. All of this was in public records during Lansing's five-month evaluation.

item.title: Lansing City Council Meeting: April 6, 2026
item.description: Deep Green withdrew. One council member read the statement she would have delivered. Thirteen residents spoke about what the seven-month fight revealed.

item.title: The Document the Council Is Voting On: Deep Green's Buy-Sell Agreement
item.description: The Deep Green buy-sell agreement is 14 pages long. The three pages that would contain binding commitments are blank.

item.title: BWL's Hot Water Conversion and Deep Green's Free Heat
item.description: Deep Green's central promise is free waste heat for BWL's hot water system. That system doesn't exist yet. The cost of converting each downtown building to receive it has never been disclosed.

item.title: Lansing's Housing Crisis: Homeowners
item.description: Lansing has the highest property tax rate in Ingham County. The lowest-value homes are over-assessed by 2x. The average house was built in 1946. For homeowners, the crisis is different but the math is just as bad.

item.title: Twenty-Three Unanswered Questions About Deep Green
item.description: The Lansing City Council votes Monday on a land sale and rezoning for the Deep Green data center. Here is what has not been disclosed, not been analyzed, and not been answered.

item.title: Fact-Checking Deep Green's Emissions Blog Post
item.description: Deep Green published a blog post claiming their fuel cells will reduce Lansing's emissions. Every material claim is false, misleading, or unverifiable. Here is the public record.

item.title: Deep Green's Parent Company Has Negative £435 Million in Net Assets
item.description: Deep Green has 1.13 megawatts of operational data center capacity. Lansing is being asked to approve 24 megawatts. The company that controls Deep Green is failing UK financial resilience requirements.

item.title: "Under Duress": Why Is Deep Green Revenue in the City Budget?
item.description: Mayor Schor tied $1 million in fire, housing, and neighborhood funding to Deep Green approval the same night as the public hearing. A council member called it duress.

item.title: Fact-Checking the Mayor's Deep Green Letter
item.description: Mayor Schor published a letter asking residents to support the Deep Green data center based on 'facts, not misinformation.' Here is what the public record says about his claims.

item.title: Lansing's Housing Crisis: Wages Fall Short
item.description: Parts 1 and 2 showed Lansing households can't cover basic needs. This post maps why: low-wage employment, compounding debt, and hidden costs that make the gap wider.

item.title: Lansing's Housing Crisis: By the Tract
item.description: The housing crisis doesn't hit Lansing evenly. Census tract data shows where income, poverty, health, and demographics cluster — and where they diverge.

item.title: Lansing's Housing Crisis: Renters
item.description: More than half of Lansing renters are cost-burdened. Rents are rising faster than anywhere in Michigan. The federal 30% affordability standard hides the real problem. Here are the numbers.

item.title: Deep Green: How Would You Vote?
item.description: Every promise, every contract, every claim — checked against the public record. Here is what council knows and what it doesn't. You decide.

item.title: 428 W Lenawee St Is a Hub for Dark Money Activity
item.description: At least $698,000 from unions, utilities, and corporate PACs has flowed into 17 nonprofits registered at a single Lansing address. The organizations told the IRS they engaged in zero political activity. Public records show attack mailers, robocalls, and racist fabrications.

item.title: Lansing: Fact-Checking the March 23 City Council Meeting
item.description: What Deep Green, the mayor, and supporters said at the March 23 City Council meeting — checked against the public record.

item.title: Socrates Is Not a Cat: A Citizen's Guide to Logical Fallacies
item.description: All cats die. Socrates is dead. Therefore Socrates is a cat. When officials sell a project, they rely on arguments that sound logical but aren't. 19 real examples from the Deep Green data center debate, named and explained so you can spot them next time.

item.title: Lansing: The Garza Conflict, Spelled Out
item.description: Lansing Council Member Jeremy Garza earns $126,742 per year from the Michigan Pipe Trades Association while voting on projects that benefit the pipe trades. The Lansing City Charter says officers with conflicts cannot vote, and the land sale needs his vote to pass.

item.title: Lansing: Bloom Energy Has a Pattern of Downplaying Toxic Waste
item.description: In 2013, Bloom Energy told a waste contractor its fuel cell canisters were nonhazardous. They contained benzene. In 2026, Bloom's VP told the Lansing City Council fuel cells generate no toxic chemicals. The EPA fined Bloom $1.16 million for hazardous waste violations.

item.title: How Consumers Energy's Dark Money Reaches Lansing City Hall
item.description: Between 2014 and 2017, Consumers Energy funneled $43.5 million into a single anonymous nonprofit. Public records trace how that money reaches Lansing City Hall through a network of 501(c)(4) organizations, a political consulting firm, and a sitting judge's former legal infrastructure.

item.title: Lansing: A Conflict Question Could Reshape the Deep Green Land Sale Vote
item.description: The Lansing City Charter requires six of eight votes to sell city property and bars members with financial interests from voting. Council Member Garza is VP of UA Local 333, which stands to benefit from the Deep Green project. If he cannot vote, the sale cannot pass.

item.title: Lansing Council: Donor Cheat Sheet
item.description: A public records lookup of campaign contributions from LRC-PAC, UA Local 333, and other influential donors to each of the eight sitting Lansing City Council members.

item.title: Can Michigan Communities Trust the Data Center Coalition's "Independent" Information?
item.description: Michigan for Responsible Data Centers says it provides neutral information to communities evaluating data center proposals. Public records show its members fund the politicians who approve those projects, through channels designed to hide the source of the money.

item.title: Michigan's New Data Center "Information" Coalition Has the Hallmarks of an Astroturf Campaign
item.description: Michigan for Responsible Data Centers launched March 19 promising 'clear, accurate information.' Its website is managed by a PR firm that represents a data center developer. Its cited economic analysis was paid for by a coalition member. Its university guidebook was reviewed by coalition members before publication. No individuals are named anywhere on the site.

item.title: Lansing: Is the Council Being Set Up to Vote on Deep Green Blind? The Public Record Says Yes.
item.description: The council votes soon on the Deep Green land sale and rezoning. Public records raise questions about undisclosed contracts, TIFA tax capture, missing studies, and an NDA that may not be legally defensible.

item.title: Deep Green's Projected $933K in Tax Revenue Does Not Reach the General Fund
item.description: LEAP projects $933,081 in annual property tax from the Deep Green data center. Michigan TIF law diverts roughly half to the TIFA before it reaches any taxing authority. The mayor was corrected on camera.

item.title: Lansing: Public Utility, Private Contract: The Deep Green Fuel Cell Deal
item.description: Deep Green would buy the fuel cells. BWL would own them. Bloom would operate them. The contracts are under NDA. Bloom's fuel cells in Delaware lasted seven years. The proposed BWL contract is twenty.

item.title: How Organic Is the Support for Deep Green?
item.description: Seven of the 12 template support letters generated through a paid advocacy platform for the Deep Green data center came from Lansing Regional Chamber members, award recipients, or policy committee participants. The Chamber published four press releases supporting the project without disclosing any of these connections.

item.title: The Lansing Chamber Funds Campaigns, Runs Advocacy, and Reports $0 in Political Spending
item.description: The Lansing Regional Chamber's IRS filing shows $311,344 in fees with no vendor names and $0 in political spending. It operates a PAC that funded 6 of 8 Council members and endorsed a US Senate candidate but does not appear in the FEC database or the IRS Form 8871 disclosure system.

item.title: Who Owns Lansing? 24 Landlords Control 946 Rental Parcels
item.description: An analysis of 42,175 Lansing tax parcels reveals 24 mega-landlords controlling 946 rental properties, with eviction filing rates exceeding 100% for six of them. 10.4% of rental parcels are owned out of state.

item.title: Lansing: BWL Steam Item Listed on Park Board Agenda, Missing from Minutes
item.description: The Lansing Park Board's December 2025 agenda listed five items including BWL Wentworth Park Steam Conversion. The minutes listed three. The missing item sits on BWL's Deep Green construction corridor. The November meeting where it was introduced has zero documents on file.

item.title: Lansing Is Michigan's Fastest-Rising Rental Market
item.description: Zillow, HUD, and Census data confirm Lansing rents rose 25.3% since 2022, outpacing every Michigan metro. Three ZIP codes saw double-digit annual increases, hitting the lowest-income neighborhoods hardest.

item.title: Lansing: Did BWL's Board Know About Deep Green When It Approved a $100M Steam Conversion?
item.description: The Lansing Board of Water and Light approved a $100M steam-to-hot-water conversion without mentioning Deep Green, the data center project whose waste heat would fill the resulting gap. The same consultant validated both sides.

item.title: Bloom Energy: Fined, Sued, and Subsidized in Three States
item.description: Bloom Energy will operate the Deep Green data center's fuel cells in Lansing. In Delaware, Bloom received $580M+ in subsidies, was fined $1.37M by the EPA, and had fuel cells decommissioned after seven years.

item.title: Lansing Chamber PAC Funded 6 of 8 Council Members
item.description: The Lansing Regional Chamber's LRC-PAC contributed $30,750 to 6 of 8 sitting Council members. Its endorsed candidates win at rates above 85%. The same executives run both the PAC and project advocacy.

item.title: Lansing Council Member Garza: Union VP Who Votes on Union Projects
item.description: Jeremy Garza is VP of UA Local 333 and a Lansing City Council member. His entire $48,050 campaign came from unions and PACs. He has never recused from a vote.

item.title: Deep Green PR Rep Was a Lansing Planning Commissioner
item.description: Josh Hovey served on the Lansing Planning Commission through June 2025. Five months later he lobbied the same body as Deep Green's paid PR representative. He sits on the PAC that funded 6 of 8 Council members.

item.title: Deep Green Support Letters Were Platform-Generated
item.description: All 12 support letters submitted to Lansing City Council for the Deep Green data center were routed through The Soft Edge, an advocacy platform. Email header forensics reveal template clusters and loopback addresses.
